SGB turns layout and process facts into a physical model, then into planned boundaries that a CAD backend can construct. A junction request also names the two terminal owners and the central lumped sheet; terminal completion exists to give that sheet real, correctly owned metal contacts at both ends. This page is the map for the method; each chapter follows one handoff from its inputs to its outputs and explains why that handoff exists.

The running example is the public notched-pad model: a left conductor with one hole, a separate right conductor on another Net, a Si substrate, surrounding air, a selected physical approximation, and an explicitly requested rectangular junction. Its source polygon has area 8 µm². The junction request adds a 1 µm² terminal support to complete the left side; it does not merge the two Nets.

::: {.callout-note title="Backend focus"}
The construction chapters follow Gmsh/OCC and Palace. AEDT shares supported source and physical meanings, then builds with its native Modeler. A CAD plan is an input to meshing; it is not itself a mesh or field solution.
:::

## The design in one model {#fig-sgb-physical}

Think of two adjacent solution volumes that share one physical face. The face is created once and referenced by both volumes with opposite orientation. The two volumes remain distinct because their materials and boundaries differ; sharing the face does not merge their identity. That small example captures the method's central rule: decide ownership and adjacency before native CAD construction.

The same rule applies to the pad. A hole is empty space inside its outer ring; the exterior notch is open to the outside. The component describes those local outlines and selectors. The process stack says which material occupies each declared layer and where it sits in Z. The assembly places occurrences, assigns final Nets and selects the physical approximation. Read [Sources](sgb/sources.qmd) before interpreting the records.

The profile changes the geometry used by a solve without rewriting the source film. For the running example, the selected `substrate_face` representation places the effective conductor sheet on the Si top face. The junction is an explicit model request: the planner completes the named terminal supports and preserves the central port surface. The [physical model chapter](sgb/physical-model.qmd) separates those decisions from their source inputs.

## From planar ownership to a shared boundary

A planar subdivision operation nodes only the relevant XY operands for that operation. Each resulting face gets a membership vector from directed ring transitions. The hole and the unbounded exterior can both be outside the conductor while still being different faces. The [planar arrangement chapter](sgb/planar-arrangement.qmd) walks through those transitions and checks their area.

After the physical faces are known, neighboring surfaces must agree on their exact boundary. A long edge on one surface is split wherever another incident boundary introduces a point; both surfaces then refer to the same atomic curves. The [shared topology chapter](sgb/shared-topology.qmd) explains point keys, loop roles and volume orientation.

## Two construction routes

Ordinary polygonal input follows the route planner, validates ownership and interfaces, canonicalizes the boundary, then lowers planned points and curves into OCC surfaces and volumes. An active source-curve declaration selects a separate curved-construction route: it creates a shared planar arrangement, retains native curve history and sweeps the complete edge complex through the selected Z levels. Both routes start from explicit source meaning; neither asks a global Boolean operation to invent that meaning.

The [CAD and mesh chapter](sgb/cad-mesh.qmd) draws the boundary between exported CAD and a later mesh. The [performance chapter](sgb/performance.qmd) explains reusable work and stage timing without treating a design hypothesis as a measured speedup. The [validation chapter](sgb/validation.qmd) shows how failures localize to the handoff that could not be established.

## Current scope and history {#distance-bands}

::: {.callout-warning title="Geometric distance bands are withdrawn"}
Current SGB does not partition a source surface into geometric distance bands. The previous design and its observations remain in the [historical distance-band page](../history/sgb-geometric-bands.qmd). Palace's native Mask/Inset input is separate; it can select a region only when the chosen executable supports that native setting. It does not make SGB cut the source geometry.
:::

## Implementation entry points

The concepts above describe the data flow. These source entry points name the corresponding public or compiler operations; they are a compact map, not a substitute for the explanations above.

| Stage | Entry point | What crosses the boundary |
|---|---|---|
| Source preparation | `GeometryPlan.prepare()` | Mutable component, PDK and assembly declarations become an immutable snapshot |
| Physical interpretation | `interpret_physical_geometry(...)` | The selected profile produces effective geometry and support/interface records |
| Boundary topology | `plan_canonical_topology(...)` | Planned surfaces become shared points, curves, edge rings and oriented references |
| Native construction | `SemanticGeometryBuilder.build(...)` | The validated plan becomes native CAD plus source/tag mapping |

See the [geometry and compiler contract](../geometry-sgb.qmd), [physical representation contract](../specs/physical-representation.qmd), and [Palace preparation contract](../specs/palace-electrostatic-sgb.qmd) for exact fields and backend handoffs.
